hints: Look at what touches the phospholipids on both sides of the cell surface membrane, watery cytoplasm inside and watery tissue fluid outside.
Remember which part of a phospholipid loves water (hydrophilic, polar) and which part hates water (hydrophobic, non-polar), then match them to inside and outside.
walkthrough:
**Picture the surroundings**

Think of the membrane sitting between two watery solutions. The inside is cytoplasm and the outside is tissue fluid, both are mostly water.

So anything facing outwards must be happy to touch water.

**Recall the two parts of a phospholipid**

Each phospholipid has a phosphate head which is polar and hydrophilic (water-loving). It also has two fatty acid tails which are non-polar and hydrophobic (water-hating).

**Put them in the right places**

The hydrophilic polar heads face outwards to touch the water on both sides. The hydrophobic non-polar tails hide away facing inwards, away from water. That matches option B perfectly.

options.A: This swaps the properties around. Phosphate heads are polar, not non-polar, and fatty acid tails are non-polar, not polar.
options.B: This is correct. Polar hydrophilic phosphate heads face outwards to water, and non-polar hydrophobic fatty acid tails face inwards away from water.
options.C: This puts the molecule back to front. Tails cannot face outwards because they are hydrophobic and would be exposed to water.
options.D: This gets both the part and the property wrong. Fatty acid tails are non-polar and face inwards, phosphate heads are polar and face outwards.
